cues.text: By the mid-fifteenth century, the once-mighty Byzantine Empire had dwindled to little more than the city of Constantinople itself and scattered outposts in the Peloponnese, hemmed in on all sides by the rapidly expanding Ottoman Empire .
Repeated Byzantine appeals for Western military aid had gone largely unanswered, in no small part because of the still-unhealed division between the Latin and Greek churches dating to 1054.
The Council of Florence and a Failed Reunion

In a last effort to secure Western help, Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos negotiated a formal reunion of the Greek and Latin churches at the Council of Florence in 1439, accepting Roman positions on the filioque and papal primacy.
The union proved deeply unpopular among the Byzantine clergy and populace, and the promised substantial Western military relief never fully materialized.
The young Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II , only twenty-one, laid siege to Constantinople in April 1453.
His army vastly outnumbered the roughly seven thousand defenders under Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos , while massive siege cannons battered the ancient Theodosian Walls for weeks.
Despite a valiant defense, the city fell to a final assault on May 29, 1453 ; Constantine XI died fighting in the breach.
The End of Rome's Eastern Half

The fall of Constantinople extinguished the last remnant of the Roman Empire, nearly 1,500 years after Augustus, and transformed the great church of Hagia Sophia — for nine centuries the heart of Byzantine Christian worship — into a mosque.
Cardinal Isidore of Kiev, sent to secure acceptance of the Florentine union, arrived too late to prevent the catastrophe he had hoped to forestall.

In the years surrounding the conquest, Greek scholars fled westward, especially to Italy, carrying with them manuscripts of classical Greek literature and philosophy that had been little known in the Latin West.
Their arrival is traditionally counted among the sparks that helped fuel the flowering of Renaissance humanism in Italian centers such as Florence and Venice.
The loss of Constantinople ended any realistic prospect of reversing the schism between East and West through the Florentine union, which the Eastern Church formally repudiated at a synod in 1484.
It also removed the last check on Ottoman expansion into the Balkans and, eventually, toward the very gates of Vienna, reshaping the map of Christian and Muslim Europe for centuries to come.
